The SPEI and the SPI are usually computed from monthly data. But
`spei()` and `spi()` work with any whole number of periods per year. The
number of periods is taken from the frequency of the time series: 12 for
monthly data, 52 for weekly data, 48 for quarter-months, 36 for ten-day
periods, and so on. The distribution of the index is fitted separately for
each period of the year, as it is for each month with monthly data.

The time scale (`scale`) then counts periods, not months. With 48 periods
per year, scales of 4, 12, 24 and 48 periods are equivalent to 1, 3, 6
and 12 months. With 52 weeks per year, 13 weeks are a quarter of a year,
and 52 weeks a full year.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)
```

## Building the periodic series

Climate data at a finer resolution than the month usually come as daily
series, which have to be aggregated into periods. The number of days in a
month or a year is not a multiple of seven, so the periods cannot all have
the same length. Two conventions are common:

- **Quarter-months**, 48 periods per year. Each month is split into four
  periods, which start on days 1, 9, 16 and 23. They span days 1-8, 9-15,
  16-22, and 23 to the end of the month, so they have 8, 7, 7, and 6 to 9
  days. This is the convention of the Spanish drought monitor
  (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2017), and of the `tarazona` dataset used below.
  The periods fit exactly into the months.
- **Weeks**, 52 periods per year. The year is split into 7-day weeks
  starting on 1 January, and the day left over at the end of the year (two
  in leap years) is added to the last week, which has 8 or 9 days.
  Functions that number the weeks of the year, such as
  `lubridate::week()`, give a 53rd week of one or two days instead. It
  should be merged with the 52nd: a period with so few days would be
  fitted separately and give unreliable values.

These functions give the period of the year of each day, with either
convention:

```{r}
# Quarter-month (1 to 48) of each date
quarter_month <- function(date) {
  day <- as.integer(format(date, "%d"))
  month <- as.integer(format(date, "%m"))
  (month - 1) * 4 + findInterval(day, c(1, 9, 16, 23))
}

# Week (1 to 52) of each date; the last week has 8 or 9 days
week52 <- function(date) {
  doy <- as.integer(format(date, "%j"))
  pmin((doy - 1) %/% 7 + 1, 52)
}
```

The daily values are then summed (precipitation, evapotranspiration) or
averaged (temperature) over each period of each year. The result is
converted to a time series with the frequency of the convention. This
function assumes that the daily series covers whole years:

```{r}
to_periods <- function(x, date, period, frequency, fun = sum) {
  year <- as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))
  v <- tapply(x, list(period, year), fun)
  ts(as.vector(v), start = c(min(year), 1), frequency = frequency)
}
```

We try them on a **synthetic** daily precipitation series of ten years,
with rain on about a third of the days:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
date <- seq(as.Date("2001-01-01"), as.Date("2010-12-31"), by = "day")
prcp_day <- rbinom(length(date), 1, 0.3) * rexp(length(date), 1 / 5)

prcp_qm <- to_periods(prcp_day, date, quarter_month(date), 48)
prcp_wk <- to_periods(prcp_day, date, week52(date), 52)
length(prcp_qm)
length(prcp_wk)
```

The totals of each year are the same with both conventions, since no day
is lost:

```{r}
all.equal(
  as.numeric(aggregate(prcp_qm, FUN = sum)),
  as.numeric(aggregate(prcp_wk, FUN = sum))
)
```

## Evapotranspiration

The potential evapotranspiration functions of the package
(`thornthwaite()`, `hargreaves()` and `penman()`) work with monthly data
only. They give an error with a time series of another frequency. For the
SPEI at a finer resolution there are two options:

- use reference evapotranspiration (ETo) or PET from another source, at
  the same resolution as the precipitation, as in the `tarazona` dataset;
- compute PET daily, for example with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation
  (Allen et al., 1998) in another package, and sum it over each period
  with `to_periods()`.

A daily version of `penman()` is a pending request for the package
(issue #6 on GitHub).

## The tarazona data

The `tarazona` dataset has the climate of an Aleppo pine plantation at
Tarazona (Spain), extracted from the Spanish drought monitor
(Vicente-Serrano et al., 2017). It has 48 quarter-months per year from 1961
to 2020. The precipitation (`PRCP`) and the ETo (`ETO`) are totals per
period, in mm, and the temperatures are means of the period. See
`?Datasets` for the details, and `vignette("scale_scan")` for the tree
growth data of the same site.

```{r}
data(tarazona)
clim <- tarazona$clim
frequency(clim)
head(clim, 8)
```

The climatic water balance is the precipitation minus the ETo:

```{r}
bal <- clim[, "PRCP"] - clim[, "ETO"]
```

## Computing the index

`spei()` is called as with monthly data. The time scales are given in
periods. Here we compute the SPEI at 4, 12, 24 and 48 quarter-months (1,
3, 6 and 12 months). The reference period is given as year and period,
from the first period of 1981 to the last period of 2010:

```{r}
scales <- c(4, 12, 24, 48)
spei_qm <- lapply(scales, function(s) {
  spei(bal, s, ref.start = c(1981, 1), ref.end = c(2010, 48),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
})
names(spei_qm) <- scales
```

The `plot` method works as with monthly data. Here, the SPEI at 12
quarter-months:

```{r, fig.alt = "SPEI at a time scale of 12 quarter-months (3 months) at Tarazona from 1961 to 2020, with positive values in blue and negative values in red, and the reference period 1981-2010 shaded"}
plot(spei_qm[["12"]])
```

The values of the index for the last ten years at the four scales:

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "SPEI at 4, 12, 24 and 48 quarter-months at Tarazona from 2011 to 2020. The series get smoother as the time scale increases."}
idx <- do.call(cbind, lapply(spei_qm, function(x) x$fitted))
colnames(idx) <- paste0("SPEI-", scales)
plot(window(idx, start = c(2011, 1)),
  main = "", xlab = "Year", type = "h",
  panel = function(x, ...) {
    lines(x, ...)
    abline(h = 0, col = "grey50")
  }
)
```

## Comparison with the monthly index

The monthly data are the sums of each group of four quarter-months:

```{r}
to_monthly <- function(x) {
  ts(colSums(matrix(x, nrow = 4)), start = start(x)[1], frequency = 12)
}
bal_m <- to_monthly(clim[, "PRCP"]) - to_monthly(clim[, "ETO"])
spei_m3 <- spei(bal_m, 3, ref.start = c(1981, 1), ref.end = c(2010, 12),
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

The SPEI at 12 quarter-months in the last period of each month covers the
same days as the SPEI at 3 months in that month. The sums are the same,
and the distribution of that period is fitted to the same values as the
distribution of the month. So the two indices are equal:

```{r}
last <- cycle(bal) %% 4 == 0
all.equal(
  as.numeric(spei_qm[["12"]]$fitted[last]),
  as.numeric(spei_m3$fitted)
)
```

The quarter-month index adds three values between each pair of monthly
values. The plot shows both series in 2011 and 2012, with each value placed
at the end of its window:

```{r, fig.alt = "SPEI at 12 quarter-months and at 3 months at Tarazona in 2011 and 2012. The monthly values coincide with every fourth quarter-month value, and the quarter-month series shows changes within each month."}
w <- window(spei_qm[["12"]]$fitted, start = c(2011, 1), end = c(2012, 48))
m <- window(spei_m3$fitted, start = c(2011, 1), end = c(2012, 12))
plot(as.numeric(time(w)) + 1 / 48, w,
  type = "l", col = "grey40",
  xlab = "Year", ylab = "SPEI"
)
points(as.numeric(time(m)) + 1 / 12, m, pch = 19, col = "red")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomleft", c("12 quarter-months", "3 months"),
  col = c("grey40", "red"), lty = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 19), bty = "n"
)
```

This equality holds because the quarter-months fit exactly into the
months. Weeks do not, so a weekly index is close to the monthly one but
not equal to it.

## Noise and the fit of the distributions

The finer resolution has some costs.

At short time scales the index changes a lot from one period to the next.
With one period (about a week) the index reflects the rain of single
events. The correlation between consecutive values (lag-1
autocorrelation) shows how fast the index changes:

```{r}
spei_1 <- spei(bal, 1, ref.start = c(1981, 1), ref.end = c(2010, 48),
  verbose = FALSE
)$fitted
lag1 <- function(x) {
  x[!is.finite(x)] <- NA
  cor(x[-1], x[-length(x)], use = "complete.obs")
}
round(c("SPEI-1" = lag1(spei_1), apply(idx, 2, lag1)), 2)
```

At one period consecutive values are only weakly correlated. At 4 periods
(one month) and more the windows of consecutive values overlap, and the
index changes more slowly.

```{r, include = FALSE}
n_inf <- sum(is.infinite(spei_1))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
zero <- tapply(clim[, "PRCP"] == 0, cycle(clim), mean)
```

The distribution of the index is fitted separately for each of the 48
periods of the year. Each fit uses one value per year, so it has as many
values as a monthly fit: 60 with the whole record, and 30 with the
reference period 1981-2010. But there are four times as many fits, each
with its own sampling error, and the values of neighbouring periods do
not inform each other. Totals over short periods are also more skewed, and
precipitation has more zeros: `r round(100 * mean(clim[, "PRCP"] == 0), 1)`%
of the quarter-months of the `tarazona` data have no precipitation (up to
`r round(100 * max(zero))`% in some periods), while all the months have
some. This matters for the SPI at short time scales. The SPEI at one
period also has `r n_inf` value outside the range of its fitted
distribution, which gives an infinite index value. See `vignette("options")`
for the treatment of zeros and of values outside the distribution.

So the fine resolution is most useful at time scales of one month or more,
to locate the start and the end of a dry spell, or the window of the year
that a variable responds to, more precisely than with monthly data.

## Finding the best window

`scale_scan()` works with any frequency too. It correlates an annual series
with the index in each period of the year and at each time scale. For
example, to scan the tree growth of the `tarazona` dataset at time scales
of 4 to 96 quarter-months (rbai being the detrended growth of the cores):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
scale_scan(bal, rbai, scales = seq(4, 96, by = 4))
```

See `vignette("scale_scan")` for the complete example.
